Faraday's Law EMF Equations for Coils, Transformers and Generators

Faraday's law EMF is the voltage induced when the magnetic flux linking a coil changes, given by EMF = minus N × dΦ/dt. The minus sign is Lenz's law, which sets the direction. The same law takes a different practical form for each machine, depending on how the flux is made to change.

ApplicationEMF equationSymbols
Coil with changing fluxEMF = N × ΔΦ ÷ ΔtN turns, ΔΦ change in flux (Wb), Δt time (s)
Conductor moving in a fieldEMF = B × l × vB flux density (T), l length (m), v speed (m/s)
Transformer winding (RMS)E = 4.44 × f × N × Φmf supply frequency (Hz), Φm peak flux (Wb)
Coil rotating in a fielde = N × B × A × ω × sin(ωt)A coil area (m²), ω angular speed (rad/s)

Worked Example: Transformer EMF

  1. Take a winding with N = 200 turns on a 50 Hz supply.
  2. Assume a peak core flux Φm = 0.01 Wb.
  3. Apply E = 4.44 × f × N × Φm.
  4. E = 4.44 × 50 × 200 × 0.01 = 444 V RMS.

The 4.44 factor comes from the sine wave: it equals 2π ÷ √2, which converts the peak rate of change of flux into an RMS voltage. The rotating coil equation shows the generator case, where the induced EMF reaches its peak N × B × A × ω when the coil plane lies along the field and passes through zero when it is at right angles to it.
